This method describes the calculation of calculating calorific value and specific 
gravity (relative density) of gaseous fuels from its components.

Natural 
gas is a vital component of the world's supply of energy. lt is one of the cleanest, 
safest, and most useful of all energy sources.

Natural 
gas 
burning 
is clean and emits lower levels of potentially harmful byproducts into the 
air.

Summary of Method

The ideal gas calorific value and ideal gas specific 
gravity (relative density) are calculated from the molar composition and the 
respective ideal gas values for the components. These 
values are then corrected to the real gas basis by means of a calculated 
compressibility factor.

Significance 
and Use

The calorific value 
is a measure of the value of a pure gas 
or a gas mixture for use as a fuel. It indicates the 
maximum amount of heat that can be obtained by burning a unit of the gas, for the use of gases as heating agents. The relative merits 
of gases from different sources and having different compositions can be 
compared readily on the basis of their calorific values. The calorific value is, 
therefore, used as a parameter for determining the price of the gas. It is also 
an essential factor in calculating the efficiencies of energy conversion devices 
such as gas-fired turbines.

The 
specific gravity 
(relative density) of gas describes whether the gas is less 
or more dense than air. This determines whether the gas will rise rapidly or 
tend to collect near the ground before dispersing after a leak or spill. It is 
an important factor in calculations concerning flow through pipes and orifices, 
and is used in calculating relationships between amounts of gas measured 
volumetrically and the corresponding mass or molar amounts.
Definitions

British 
Thermal Unit (Symbol Btu)

It's defined as the quantity of heat required to raise the 
temperature of one pound of water through one degree Fahrenheit (60 61oF).
1 kcal = 3.968 B.Th.U.

or 1 
B.Th.U = 252 cal = 0.252 kcal.

Compressibility 
Factor (Z )

The ratio of the actual volume of a given 
quantity of gas at a specified temperature and pressure to its volume calculated 
from the ideal gas law at the same conditions.
Gross or High Calorific Value of a Gas

The total 
amount of heat produced when one unit of the fuel has been burnt completely and 
the products of combustion have been cooled to room temperature of usually 60oF 
(15.6oC).
Lower or Net Calorific Value of a Gas

The net heat 
produced when unit mass/volume of the fuel is burnet completely and the products 
are permit to escape. Alternatively net or lower calorific value:
= Gross C.V. - latent heat of water vapour formed

= Gross C.V. - 
Mass of hydrogen 9 latent heat of steam

because 1 part by mass 
of hydrogen 
produces 9 parts 
by mass of water. The latent heat of steam is 587 
kcal/kg or 1060 B.Th.U./Ib of water vapour formed at room temperature i.e.15oC.
Specific Gravity (Relative Density)

The ratio of the density of the gaseous fuel, under specific conditions of temperature and pressure 
to the density of dry air of normal carbon dioxide content, at the same 
temperature and pressure.
Safety Precautions

This method may involve the use of hazardous materials, operations, and 
equipment. It's the responsibility of whoever uses this method to establish 
appropriate safety practices and to determine the applicability of 
regulatory limitations prior to use.
